documents.title: Large Language Models Versus Static Code Analysis Tools: A Systematic Benchmark for Vulnerability Detection
documents.venue: arXiv preprint; manuscript text refers to itself as a thesis, so provenance is a degree thesis adapted to preprint
documents.license_redistribution: permitted with attribution; share-alike propagates to derivative compilations
documents.peer_review_status: not peer reviewed; no venue stated

datasets.name: curated suite of 10 real-world C# projects
datasets.limitations: small N, single language, single run per configuration, no variance or confidence intervals reported, default tool configurations

technical_architecture: SARIF 2.1.0 as the common result interchange format
SonarQube, CodeQL, Snyk Code as rule-based comparators
GPT-4.1, Mistral Large, DeepSeek V3 via GitHub Models platform

results.mapping_note: verified: the paper states the static-tool mapping explicitly in Section V ("SonarQube, CodeQL, and SnykCode - achieved average F1 scores of 0.260, 0.386, and 0.546, respectively") and the LLM mapping in the same sentence pair. Previously inferred from abstract ordering.
results.false_positive_observation: DeepSeek V3 exhibits the highest false-positive ratio
results.localization_failure: all three LLMs reported an incorrect line/column region in SARIF output; all correctly identified the file; authors found no correlation among the localization errors and attribute them to BPE tokenisation
results.latency: CodeQL slowest of the static tools; attributed to loading and processing large predefined rule sets

negative_results: LLM line/column localization failed universally, which the authors state may preclude LLM use where SARIF location is required
Hallucinated findings where currently-current dependency versions were reported as outdated
statistical_limitations: no repeated runs, so no variance estimate
63 vulnerabilities is too few for stable per-CWE conclusions

reproducibility.notes: authors state an open benchmark and JSON-based result harness were released; URL not verified in this pass

documents.peer_review_tier_basis: Thesis preprint; no venue and no peer review.

documents.title: Outside the Comfort Zone: Analysing LLM Capabilities in Software Vulnerability Detection

versions.note: accepted to ESORICS 2024 per comments field

documents.peer_review_status: peer reviewed, ESORICS 2024, per the manuscript header; publisher record not opened

datasets.authored: one dataset compiled by the authors
datasets.limitations: binary vulnerable/non-vulnerable formulation only, no vulnerability-type labels

results.accuracy_variation: significant variation in classification accuracy across benchmarks
results.fine_tuning_effect: fine-tuning lets small models outperform larger ones, but only within the specific scenarios they were trained on
results.generalization: models do not generalise well to different testing environments
results.label_quality_finding_primary: Semgrep, used as an independent oracle, identified only a very small fragment of the vulnerabilities each dataset claims to contain
results.label_quality_finding_secondary: Semgrep identified vulnerabilities inside code that datasets labelled secure, in several datasets
attributed_causes_of_mislabelling: treating code as fixed after a commit even where the vulnerability was not resolved

negative_results: answer to 'can base LLMs detect vulnerabilities in source code' recorded by the authors as unclear
larger models more stable across datasets but still not strong
statistical_limitations: binary classification collapses severity and type
benchmark label noise is unquantified beyond the Semgrep cross-check, and Semgrep itself has unknown recall on these samples
documents.security_implications_noted_by_authors: training on mislabelled data functions analogously to data poisoning
documents.peer_review_tier_basis: ESORICS 2024 acceptance stated in the arXiv comments field. No publisher record opened.

documents.title: Large Language Model for Vulnerability Detection and Repair: Literature Review and the Road Ahead
documents.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM), May 2025
documents.peer_review_status: peer reviewed, TOSEM, per external citations; publisher record not opened
documents.datasets_analyzed: surveys datasets used by primary studies; notes prevalence of synthetic data for repair and real-world data lacking test cases
key_contributions_extracted: Split of LLM adaptation techniques into detection adaptation and repair adaptation
Six enumerated limitations of existing studies
enumerated_limitations: L1 Small input granularity (function-level dominance; cross-function and cross-repository cases overlooked)
L2 Lack of high-quality vulnerability datasets (noisy and incorrect labels from automatic collection; manual checking expensive)
L3 Suboptimal performance from complexity in vulnerability data
L5 Lack of deployment consideration (notably IDE and workflow integration)
L6 Lack of high accuracy and robustness
documents.retained_for: detection/repair adaptation split; limitation taxonomy as a cross-check
documents.peer_review_tier_basis: TOSEM publication reported by citing works. Publisher record not opened.
